name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q01 - Contrasting traits studied by Mendel in pea

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Characters in garden pea) with List II (Contrasting traits studied by Mendel) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Stem height(i) Inflated / constricted
B. Flower colour(ii) Tall / dwarf
C. Pod shape(iii) Yellow / green
D. Seed colour(iv) Violet / white

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel selected \(14\) true-breeding pea plant varieties representing \(7\) pairs of contrasting traits for his hybridisation experiments.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Character
For stem height, the contrasting traits are tall (dominant) and dwarf (recessive). For flower colour, the contrasting traits are violet (dominant) and white (recessive). For pod shape, the contrasting traits are inflated/full (dominant) and constricted (recessive). For seed colour, the contrasting traits are yellow (dominant) and green (recessive).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each character with its contrasting trait pair gives: A–(ii), B–(iv), C–(i), D–(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q02 - Fundamental genetic terms and their definitions

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Genetic Terms) with List II (Descriptions) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Alleles(i) Physical expression or appearance of a character
B. Genotype(ii) Slightly different forms of the same gene coding for contrasting traits
C. Phenotype(iii) Genetic constitution of an organism such as \(TT\) or \(Tt\)
D. Test cross(iv) Crossing a dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive parent

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendelian genetics uses precise terminology to distinguish between the hereditary units, their allelic variants, the genetic makeup of an organism, its observable traits, and experimental crosses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Term
Alleles are slightly different forms of the same gene that code for a pair of contrasting traits. Genotype refers to the allelic pair of genes present in an organism (such as \(TT\), \(Tt\), or \(tt\)), whereas phenotype refers to the descriptive physical appearance (such as tall or dwarf). A test cross involves crossing an organism showing a dominant phenotype (whose genotype is unknown) with a homozygous recessive parent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs are: A–(ii), B–(iii), C–(i), D–(iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q03 - Inheritance patterns and their classic examples

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Inheritance Patterns) with List II (Examples) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Incomplete dominance(i) ABO blood grouping in humans
B. Co-dominance(ii) Flower colour in snapdragon
C. Polygenic inheritance(iii) Phenylketonuria in humans
D. Pleiotropy(iv) Human skin colour

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Several inheritance patterns extend beyond simple Mendelian complete dominance, involving intermediate phenotypes, simultaneous expression of alleles, multiple genes, or single genes with multiple effects.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pattern
Flower colour in snapdragon (Antirrhinum sp.) is a classic example of incomplete dominance, where \(Rr\) heterozygotes are pink. ABO blood grouping in humans demonstrates co-dominance because \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) both express their sugars in \(I^A I^B\) individuals. Human skin colour is a polygenic trait controlled by multiple genes with additive effects. Phenylketonuria is an example of pleiotropy, where a single gene mutation causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(ii), B–(i), C–(iv), D–(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q04 - Scientists and their major contributions in genetics

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Scientists) with List II (Contributions) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Reginald C. Punnett(i) Discovered the 'X body' during spermatogenesis in insects
B. Sutton and Boveri(ii) Developed a graphical square to calculate offspring genotype probabilities
C. Alfred Sturtevant(iii) Formulated the chromosomal theory of inheritance
D. Henking(iv) Used recombination frequency to map gene positions on a chromosome

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Modern genetics developed through key cytological, mathematical, and experimental breakthroughs following Mendel's work.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Scientist
Reginald C. Punnett developed the Punnett Square, a graphical representation for calculating the probabilities of all possible genotypes in a genetic cross. Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted the parallel behaviour of chromosomes and genes during meiosis and formulated the chromosomal theory of inheritance. Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequencies between gene pairs on the same chromosome to construct genetic maps. Henking (\(1891\)) traced a specific nuclear structure in insect spermatogenesis and named it the 'X body'.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(ii), B–(iii), C–(iv), D–(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q05 - Organisms and their chromosomal sex determination mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Organisms) with List II (Sex-Determination Mechanisms) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Grasshopper(i) \(ZW\)–\(ZZ\) (female heterogamety)
B. Drosophila(ii) \(XO\)–\(XX\) (male heterogamety)
C. Birds(iii) Haplodiploid system
D. Honey bee(iv) \(XY\)–\(XX\) (male heterogamety)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromosomal sex determination varies across animal groups, involving male heterogamety (\(XO\) or \(XY\)), female heterogamety (\(ZW\)), or chromosome-set number (haplodiploidy).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism
Grasshoppers exhibit the \(XO\) type of sex determination, where males have one X chromosome and females have two (\(XX\)). Drosophila (like humans) shows the \(XY\) type, with \(XY\) males and \(XX\) females. Birds exhibit female heterogamety, where females are \(ZW\) and males are \(ZZ\). Honey bees follow the haplodiploid system, where diploid females (\(32\) chromosomes) develop from fertilised eggs and haploid males (\(16\) chromosomes) develop parthenogenetically from unfertilised eggs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(ii), B–(iv), C–(i), D–(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q06 - Mendelian disorders and their genetic or biochemical basis

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Mendelian Disorders) with List II (Genetic / Biochemical Basis) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Haemophilia(i) Lack of enzyme converting phenylalanine into tyrosine
B. Sickle-cell anaemia(ii) Defect in either red or green cone of the eye
C. Phenylketonuria(iii) Substitution of Glutamic acid by Valine at sixth position of \(\beta\)-globin
D. Colour blindness(iv) Defect in a single protein of the blood clotting cascade

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendelian disorders are caused by alteration or mutation in a single gene, leading to specific biochemical or physiological defects.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Disorder
Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder in which a single protein involved in the clotting of blood is affected, causing non-stop bleeding from simple cuts. Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by the substitution of Glutamic acid (\(\text{Glu}\)) by Valine (\(\text{Val}\)) at the sixth position of the \(\beta\)-globin chain of haemoglobin. Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism where the individual lacks the enzyme converting phenylalanine into tyrosine. Colour blindness is an X-linked recessive defect in either the red or green cone of the eye.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(iv), B–(iii), C–(i), D–(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q07 - Chromosomal disorders with karyotype and clinical features

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Chromosomal Conditions) with List II (Karyotype / Characteristic Features) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Down's syndrome(i) \(45\) with \(XO\); sterile female with rudimentary ovaries
B. Klinefelter's syndrome(ii) \(47\), \(XXY\); overall masculine development with gynaecomastia
C. Turner's syndrome(iii) Trisomy of chromosome \(21\); furrowed tongue and broad palm crease
D. Polyploidy(iv) Increase in a whole set of chromosomes due to failure of cytokinesis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromosomal disorders result from the absence, excess, or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes (aneuploidy) or an increase in an entire chromosome set (polyploidy).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome \(21\) (\(47\) chromosomes), characterised by short stature, furrowed tongue, broad palm with characteristic palm crease, and retarded physical and mental development. Klinefelter's syndrome results from an extra X chromosome (\(47\), \(XXY\)), producing a sterile male with overall masculine development along with breast development (gynaecomastia). Turner's syndrome results from the absence of one X chromosome (\(45\) with \(XO\)), producing a sterile female with rudimentary ovaries. Polyploidy occurs when failure of cytokinesis after telophase increases the whole set of chromosomes, commonly seen in plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(iii), B–(ii), C–(i), D–(iv).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q08 - Genetic crosses and their expected phenotypic ratios

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Genetic Crosses) with List II (Expected Phenotypic Ratios) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. Monohybrid \(F_2\) (complete dominance)(i) \(1:2:1\)
B. Monohybrid \(F_2\) (incomplete dominance)(ii) \(9:3:3:1\)
C. Dihybrid \(F_2\) (independent assortment)(iii) \(1:1\)
D. Test cross of a monohybrid heterozygote(iv) \(3:1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different genetic crosses yield characteristic phenotypic ratios depending on dominance relationships, the number of independently assorting genes, and the genotypes of the parents.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Cross
In a Mendelian monohybrid cross with complete dominance (\(Tt \times Tt\)), the \(F_2\) phenotypic ratio is \(3:1\) (three-fourths tall and one-fourth dwarf). In incomplete dominance (such as \(Rr \times Rr\) in snapdragon), the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, giving a \(1:2:1\) phenotypic ratio. In a dihybrid cross with independent assortment (\(RrYy \times RrYy\)), combining \((3:1)(3:1)\) yields the \(F_2\) phenotypic ratio \(9:3:3:1\). In a test cross of a monohybrid heterozygote (\(Ww \times ww\)), half the offspring are dominant and half are recessive, giving a \(1:1\) ratio.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(iv), B–(i), C–(ii), D–(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MATCH_Q09 - Thalassemia genetics and Drosophila recombination frequencies

questiontext.text:
Match List I (Genetic Features) with List II (Specific Details) and select the correct option:

List I List II
A. \(\alpha\)-Thalassemia(i) Controlled by single gene \(HBB\) on chromosome \(11\)
B. \(\beta\)-Thalassemia(ii) Controlled by two closely linked genes \(HBA1\) and \(HBA2\) on chromosome \(16\)
C. Genes \(y\) and \(w\) in Drosophila(iii) \(37.2\%\) recombination frequency
D. Genes \(w\) and \(m\) in Drosophila(iv) \(1.3\%\) recombination frequency

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Specific human genetic disorders are mapped to defined chromosomes and loci, just as linked genes in Drosophila exhibit characteristic recombination frequencies reflecting their physical separation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Feature
\(\alpha\)-Thalassemia is controlled by two closely linked genes, \(HBA1\) and \(HBA2\), on chromosome \(16\) of each parent, whereas \(\beta\)-Thalassemia is controlled by a single gene, \(HBB\), on chromosome \(11\) of each parent. In Morgan's linkage experiments in Drosophila, the tightly linked genes for yellow body (\(y\)) and white eye (\(w\)) showed only \(1.3\%\) recombination, while the more loosely linked genes for white eye (\(w\)) and miniature wing (\(m\)) showed \(37.2\%\) recombination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: A–(ii), B–(i), C–(iv), D–(iii).
